themes.theme: Documentation and information supplied to supervisors on request
themes.definition: Duties on operators to keep documentation, logs and data available and to hand them to supervisors on (reasoned) request, together with the matching access powers.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Act's main answerability mechanism is documentation available on demand rather than routine reporting. Providers keep technical documentation, quality-management records and declarations at the disposal of national competent authorities for ten years, with Member States ensuring this survives a provider's insolvency (Art. 18); on reasoned request, providers, authorised representatives, importers and distributors must supply everything needed to demonstrate conformity, including automatically generated logs (Arts 21-24), and a provider that self-classifies a system as not high-risk must hand over that assessment (Art. 6(4); Omnibus recital 22). Market surveillance authorities get 'full access' to documentation and to training, validation and testing datasets, and to source code on reasoned request where needed to assess conformity (Art. 74(12)-(13)); law enforcement, immigration or asylum authorities that are themselves providers must let their authority access documentation immediately (Art. 78(3)); and national fundamental-rights bodies may request any documentation on Annex III systems (Art. 77, extended by the Omnibus to machine-readable electronic access). General-purpose model providers keep documentation of the model's 'training and testing process and the results of its evaluation' for the AI Office and national authorities (Art. 53(1)(a); EU088) and must cooperate, as must deployers (Art. 26(12)); EU121 Signatories give documentation and access to their marking and detection tools on request, and the ECA commits, as a deployer, to keep documentation to demonstrate conformity. Supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to authorities is fineable up to EUR 7 500 000 or 1% (Art. 99(5)). [inference] For public bodies as deployers, these passages give regulators access to providers' records but say little about what deployers themselves must hold.
themes.holders: Providers, authorised representatives, importers and distributors of high-risk systems; deployers; law enforcement, immigration and asylum authorities acting as providers; providers of general-purpose AI models; notified bodies (via Art. 11 documentation); EU121 Signatories; the ECA as deployer. Recipients: market surveillance authorities, national competent authorities, notified bodies, the AI Office and national fundamental-rights bodies.
themes.binding: Statutory duties ('shall'), mostly triggered 'upon a reasoned request'; breaches are fineable under Art. 99(4), and misleading information under Art. 99(5). Recital 101 uses 'should'; the EU121 code uses 'will' for Signatories; the ECA passage is a commitment.
themes.checks: Access to source code (Art. 74(13)): trigger: reasoned request where access is necessary to assess conformity with Chapter III Section 2 and other testing or auditing based on the data and documentation is not enough [the input note is truncated]; compared against: the Chapter III Section 2 requirements; metric or threshold: not stated; who: the market surveillance authority; what happens with the result: not stated in these passages. Model documentation includes 'the results of its evaluation', but no metric or threshold is stated.

themes.definition: Duties to enter providers, systems, public-sector uses and real-world tests in the EU database run by the Commission, and the rules on what is public.
themes.what_is_set_out: Before placing an Annex III high-risk system on the market, the provider or its authorised representative registers itself and the system in the EU database (Art. 49(1)); a provider that concludes under Art. 6(3) that an Annex III system is not high-risk must also register it, in the AI Act with 'a short summary of the grounds' (Art. 49(2), Annex VIII B). Deployers that are public authorities, Union bodies or persons acting for them must, before use, 'register themselves, select the system and register its use' (Art. 49(3), 26(8)), and their entry includes a summary of the fundamental rights impact assessment findings (Annex VIII C); entries name the natural persons responsible for registering who have legal authority to represent the provider or deployer, and must be kept up to date. The database is public, 'user-friendly' and machine-readable (Art. 71(4), Recital 131), except that registrations for law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control go into a secure non-public section open only to the Commission and national authorities, and Annex III point 2 systems are registered at national level. Registration is a precondition for authorising police real-time biometric identification, with an urgency exception (Art. 5(2); EU043), real-world tests are registered too, and market surveillance authorities may use the database as a basis for checks (Art. 80(8)). The Omnibus keeps registration of self-classified systems as 'crucial for effective market surveillance and public accountability' but says it 'should be simplified', deleting Annex VIII B points 7 and 9 (per the coder note), which removes the published grounds the AI Act required. The recitals use 'should'; the Articles use 'shall'.
themes.holders: Providers or their authorised representatives; providers that self-classify Annex III systems as not high-risk; deployers that are public authorities, Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies, or persons acting on their behalf; law enforcement authorities using real-time biometric identification; providers and prospective providers testing in real-world conditions; the natural persons responsible for registering.
themes.binding: Statutory duties (Arts 49, 71 and 26(8)), 'before' placing on the market or before use. Failure to register is formal non-compliance (Art. 83(1)(e)), on which the market surveillance authority requires the provider to end the non-compliance and may then restrict or prohibit the system; deployers' Art. 26 duties are fineable up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3%, subject to national rules on fining public bodies (Art. 99(8)). For police biometric identification, use is not to be authorised without registration except in urgency. Recitals and the Omnibus recital are non-binding.
themes.checks: Art. 80(8): trigger: not stated beyond the authority's discretion; compared against: information stored in the database, including the Art. 6(3) grounds for treating a system as not high-risk; metric or threshold: not stated; who: market surveillance authorities; what happens with the result: evaluation and, if misclassified, an order to comply and fines (Art. 80). Registration itself is not a check on the tool.

themes.theme: AI registers and inventories outside the AI Act database
themes.definition: Registers, inventories and lists of AI systems in use that public bodies are told or advised to keep, separate from the AI Act's EU database.
themes.what_is_set_out: The Commission commits internally (AI@EC) to 'establish and maintain an up-to-date register of AI systems in use at the Commission, assessed against corporate guidelines and legal requirements', from Q2 2024 and then continuously; whether the register is published is not stated. The EDPS asks EU institutions, as best practice, to keep 'a specific inventory' of generative AI systems and applications alongside their records of processing. The JRC's 2025 report recommends that public administrations 'establish and maintain public AI registries' and algorithmic registries disclosing where AI is used, for what purposes and under what governance arrangements, as a way to increase accountability. The Commission's prohibition guidelines suggest that national laws on police biometric identification include 'a central register' of uses with a summary of the substantive elements, without saying who keeps it or whether it is public. [inference] These registers would cover AI in use generally, which is wider than the AI Act's database of high-risk systems, but none of them has binding content, publication or consequence.
themes.holders: The ISG-AI and corporate governance boards (Commission); controllers and EUIs (EDPS); public administrations and Member States (JRC, holder not named in the passage); Member States through national law (EU043).
themes.binding: An internal Commission policy action; a best practice (EDPS); suggestions ('could be', 'might', JRC); suggested content for national law (EU043). No consequence is stated.

themes.theme: Records of processing and decision documentation
themes.definition: Duties under data protection law to document AI processing, roles, purposes, risk decisions and data lineage so that the controller can show compliance.
themes.what_is_set_out: The EDPS asks EU institutions to ensure generative AI processing is 'thoroughly documented' in their records of processing under Article 31 EUDPR, including the controller, processor or joint-controller roles assigned along the supply chain and, as part of the purpose, the type of model, its expected functionalities and its deployment context. All actors in a data protection impact assessment 'must ensure that any decision and action is properly documented, covering the entire generative AI system lifecycle', including risk measures and later reviews, and EU institutions should document their mitigation measures and their final assessment. Processing should be 'traceable and auditable' with supporting documentation, and traceable records of personal data and of dataset use help individuals exercise their rights. The Omnibus adds a specific record: where providers (and, through Art. 4a(2), deployers) of high-risk systems process special-category data to detect and correct bias, the records must give the reasons this was 'strictly necessary' and why other data could not achieve it. To whom these records are available and what follows if they are missing are not stated [inference: the EDPS or another supervisory authority, on request].
themes.holders: EUIs and other controllers; all actors involved in a DPIA; providers of high-risk AI systems and, through Art. 4a(2), deployers (Omnibus).
themes.binding: Restated statutory duties ('must', 'ensure') inside non-binding EDPS guidance, with some steps only encouraged ('may support'); the Omnibus record is a statutory condition when the Art. 4a power to process special-category data is used. Consequences are not stated.
themes.checks: DPIA records cover 'the subsequent reviews to be carried out' (per the coder note): trigger, comparator, metric or threshold and who: not stated; result: documented. themes.definition: Duties on providers, deployers and general-purpose model providers to report serious incidents, non-compliance and corrective action to regulators.
themes.what_is_set_out: Providers of high-risk systems must report any serious incident to the market surveillance authority of the Member State where it occurred (Art. 73(1)), with a deadline of 'not later than 15 days' after awareness (per the coder note), and must not alter the system in a way that could affect later evaluation of the incident's causes before informing the authorities (Art. 73(6)). Deployers that identify a serious incident must 'immediately inform first the provider, and then the importer or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authorities' (Art. 26(5)), and providers that find a system non-compliant must investigate with the reporting deployer and tell the authority and notified body what was wrong and what corrective action was taken (Art. 20(2)). Serious incidents during real-world testing are reported under Art. 73, and the Omnibus redirects incident reports for systems under AI Office competence to the AI Office. General-purpose model providers with systemic risk must track, document and report serious incidents and possible corrective measures to the AI Office (Art. 55(1)(c), Recital 115); EU088 reads this to include serious cybersecurity breaches and says the AI Office 'expects proactive reporting'. The ENISA paper's call for defenders 'to reliably hit 24-hour notifications' concerns cyber incidents involving AI used by attackers and is an edge case for this cell.
themes.holders: Providers of high-risk AI systems; deployers; providers and prospective providers testing in real-world conditions; providers of high-risk systems within AI Office competence; providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk; 'Defenders' (ENISA).
themes.binding: Statutory duties in the AI Act and Omnibus; consequences are not stated in these Articles, but breaches of the provider (Art. 16) and deployer (Art. 26) duties are fineable via Art. 99(4), and model providers via Art. 101. Recitals use 'should'; EU088 'expects'; ENISA recommends.
themes.checks: Trigger: a serious incident, or a finding of non-compliance, after the system is in use (ongoing); compared against: the Art. 3(49) definition of a serious incident (which covers death or serious harm to health and serious disruption of critical infrastructure, among others) and the AI Act requirements; metric or threshold: time limits only (immediately; not later than 15 days); who: the provider investigates, with the reporting deployer where applicable; what happens with the result: a report to the market surveillance authority and notified body, corrective action, and no alteration of the system before the authority is informed.

themes.theme: Prior authorisation and use-by-use reporting for police biometric identification
themes.definition: The chain by which a law enforcement authority using real-time (or post) remote biometric identification must obtain authorisation, give reasons, register, log and notify each use, and by which regulators report onward.
themes.what_is_set_out: Use of real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement should be authorised only if the authority has completed a fundamental rights impact assessment and registered the system (Recital 34; Art. 5(2)), and each request must be 'reasoned' (Art. 5(3)). In urgency, use may start without prior authorisation or registration, but authorisation must be requested 'without undue delay and at the latest within 24 hours' with reasons for the delay; if refused, use stops and the data are deleted, and EU043 adds that processing logs should show the authority the request was timely, that supervisory authorities should be able to check the stop-and-delete afterwards, and that a trustee may hold the data while a refusal is challenged. Each use is notified to the market surveillance and national data protection authorities (Art. 5(4)), which report annually to the Commission on a template (the EDPS for Union bodies), and the Commission publishes aggregated annual reports and will publish Member States' enabling laws, which must be notified within 30 days. For post-remote identification, each use is documented in the police file and made available to the authorities on request, and deployers report annually (Art. 26(10)). EU043 suggests that national laws provide for auditing of submissions 'including the technical details and accuracy criteria' before and after use, sanctions, the names of the deployer's responsible staff, a right to appeal a refusal, the rights of people searched and captured, and a central register. Recital 130 also lets law enforcement and civil protection authorities put a high-risk system into service without market surveillance authorisation if they request it during or after use.
themes.holders: Law enforcement authorities as deployers; the judicial or independent administrative authority that authorises use; market surveillance authorities and national data protection authorities; the EDPS (for Union bodies); the Commission; Member States; civil protection authorities (Recital 130).
themes.binding: Art. 5 and Art. 26(10) are statutory; recitals use 'should'; EU043 is non-binding interpretation, and its list of national-law contents is only suggested. Consequence of a refused authorisation: use stops immediately and the data are deleted. Consequences for failing to notify or report: not stated.

Logs: compared against the 24-hour deadline; who: the authorising authority; result: substantiates timeliness. Post-fact check of stop-and-delete: trigger: a refused authorisation; who: supervisory authorities; result: not stated.

themes.theme: Fundamental rights impact assessment: notification and complaint arrangements
themes.definition: The accountability side of the fundamental rights impact assessment (FRIA): notifying the regulator of its results, publishing a summary, and setting out internal governance and complaint mechanisms.
themes.what_is_set_out: Deployers that are bodies governed by public law, or private bodies providing public services, must set out in their FRIA 'the measures to be taken in the case of the materialisation of those risks, including the arrangements for internal governance and complaint mechanisms' (Art. 27(1)(f)); Recital 96 gives 'complaint handling and redress procedures' as an example of such measures. After the assessment the deployer notifies the market surveillance authority of the results on the template (Art. 27(3), Recital 96), and a summary of the findings goes into the deployer's public EU database entry (Annex VIII C point 4). For police biometric identification, EU043 asks the deployer to explain redress measures, governance procedures and complaint mechanisms 'such as in the case of a misidentification'. The content of the complaint mechanism is left to the deployer, and Art. 27 is not among the provisions listed for fines in Art. 99(4) (per the coder notes). [inference] The full assessment goes to the regulator, not the public; the public sees only the database summary, and not even that for law enforcement, migration, asylum and border uses, which are registered in the non-public section.
themes.holders: Deployers that are bodies governed by public law or private entities providing public services; law enforcement deployers of real-time biometric identification (EU043).
themes.binding: Art. 27 is statutory, with an exemption possible in the Art. 46(1) derogation case; Recital 96 and EU043 use 'should'. Consequences are not stated, and Art. 27 is not listed in Art. 99(4).

themes.theme: General-purpose model systemic-risk notification, designation and reassessment
themes.definition: Duties on general-purpose AI model providers to notify the Commission when a model meets the systemic-risk threshold, and the provider's routes to argue against, or seek reassessment of, designation.
themes.what_is_set_out: A provider whose general-purpose model meets, or will meet, the systemic-risk threshold must notify the Commission 'without delay and in any event within two weeks' (Art. 52(1), Recital 112), possibly before training ends, with compute reported in FLOP (EU088); failure to notify can lead to designation and fines under Art. 101. With the notification the provider may argue that the model 'exceptionally' does not present systemic risks, with the burden of evidence on the provider; on rejection, the Commission's decision must give reasons, and the provider has a right to be heard through a draft decision and a right of access to its file. An acceptance decision requires the provider to renotify if the underlying facts change substantially or the decision rested on incomplete or misleading information, and downstream modifiers whose modified model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities must notify as providers. A designated provider may ask for reassessment after six months with 'objective, detailed and new reasons'; the Commission 'shall take the request into account and may decide to reassess', which leaves reassessment discretionary. The Commission publishes and updates the list of systemic-risk models, and for models already on the market EU088 expected notification within two weeks of 2 August 2025, with enforcement by fines from 2 August 2026.
themes.holders: Providers of general-purpose AI models that meet or will meet the systemic-risk threshold; designated providers; downstream modifiers who become providers; the Commission (AI Office).
themes.binding: Statutory (Art. 52) with fines under Art. 101; recitals use 'should'; EU088 is non-binding interpretation and sets transitional expectations ('are expected to'). The Commission's reassessment is discretionary ('may decide').
